finding.claim: Stored indirect SSRF: the iconUrl supplied to PUT /profile is stored with no validation and later fetched by the nightly sync job with a GET. The attacker controls scheme, host, port and path, so they can target internal services or cloud metadata (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/). The response is read as a byte array, but it is not obviously returned to the caller, so this is probably blind or semi-blind. Severity is MEDIUM to HIGH depending on the privilege needed to call PUT /profile and on whether the stored bytes are later exposed. java.net.http.HttpClient does not follow redirects by default, but that does not matter because the initial host is already attacker-chosen.

trace.note: update(String webhook, String icon) receives the user-supplied icon URL from PUT /profile
this.iconUrl = icon; stored with no validation. Only `webhook` is checked, at line 12.
nightly job sync(HttpClient c) runs later and reads the stored iconUrl
URI.create(iconUrl) is passed to HttpClient.send as a GET with no allowlist, scheme check or re-validation

finding.guards_checked: No validation exists for iconUrl in update() or sync(). The regex at line 12 applies only to `webhook`. There is no scheme restriction, host allowlist, IP/CIDR blocking or re-validation at fetch time. No egress controls are present in the repo. The client's default no-redirect behavior is not a guard, because the user already chooses the initial host.

verdict.reason: src/Profile.java:16 stores the `icon` argument from update() (line 11) unvalidated (the line 12 regex covers only `webhook`), and sync() passes it straight to URI.create(iconUrl) in a GET at line 23 with no scheme or host guard. The repo has no handler or middleware showing what privilege PUT /profile needs, so the source is assumed to be user-controlled.
